newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU summit seeks to clear single currency hurdles.
newsitem.headline: EU summit seeks to clear single currency hurdles.

text.p: European Union leaders were locked in a hard-fought wrangle over conditions for a single European currency on Friday at a summit which was meant to take fresh strides towards monetary union in 1999.

After finance ministers came close to agreement on a pact to enforce budget discipline in marathon talks that ended at 3 a.m. (0300 GMT), the 15 leaders debated the path to monetary union at the first session of their summit in the Irish capital.
"The accord has been virtually reached. We are satisfied that great progress has been made," Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi told reporters just before the start.
But the leaders quickly ran into problems over German demands for tough conditions for any exemption from penalties on countries which exceed budget deficit limits after joining the single currency.

The summit went into recess while German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and French President Jacques Chirac tried to thrash out their differences on the definition of such "exceptional circumstances", with help from Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker, an EU diplomat said.

The leaders earlier formally confirmed Dutch central bank governor Wim Duisenberg as head of the institution which is set to become the future European central bank and which will control monetary policy for the euro. He will take over from Belgian Alexandre Lamfalussy from next July.
Later on Friday, the European Monetary Institute was due to unveil symbolically the first euro banknotes, which will enter the pockets of hundreds of millions of Europeans from 2002.
But heads of state and government first had to settle the elusive details of the stability pact on budget discipline.
Germany, whose citizens are wary of giving up the hard deutschemark for the untried euro, has pressed for watertight hefty sanctions on any country that overspends.
A compromise proposal drafted by finance ministers in 11-hour talks during the night fell well short of Bonn's original demands for automatic fines on budget sinners.

EU sources said Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn had warned his colleagues that failure to agree on a stability pact could hurt prospects for the introduction of the euro and give heart to those who sought to prevent it happening.

The compromise drafted on the central issue of exceptional circumstances that would justify breaching the deficit limit of three percent of gross domestic product would leave a final political judgment to the EU's council of ministers -- a key French demand.
"We have an agreement on the architecture of the stability pact," a confident French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said. "There is nothing left which is of a nature to prevent an agreement."
Financial markets seemed satisfied initially with the emerging deal but were looking for a quick endorsement from the EU leaders.

The European Commission launched a publicity campaign to ease public acceptance of the new currency earlier this week, unveiling a dollar-style symbol -- a "c" with two horizantal dashes through it -- which it is to represent the euro.

The growing sense of inevitability about monetary union could make this an uncomfortable summit for British Prime Minister John Major, whose Conservative government, deeply torn over European policy, lost its parliamentary majority on Thursday when the opposition Labour party won a by-election.
Major, facing an election by May, is under strong pressure from Eurosceptics in his party to end his wait-and-see approach to monetary union and rule out joining the single currency.

The British leader will also be seeking to resist any move towards closer European integration on the summit's other main agenda item -- a drive to reform EU institutions in preparation for admitting former communist central European countries from around the year 2000.

The Irish presidency of the EU has produced a report to increase cooperation in foreign, defence, interior and justice affairs but it has left aside for now the issue of greater majority voting most sensitive to Britain.
"I don't think it's going to be a summit in which serious decisions are going to be taken," Major told reporters.

France and Germany put forward their own proposals for greater integration on Monday, saying it was vital to give the slow-moving negotiations new momentum if a substantial reform is to be achieved by the deadline of next June in Amsterdam.
